author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
occasion: A homily exhorting the congregation to practice a true, God-pleasing fast, probably delivered in connection with a fasting season or commemoration.
argument: Fasting is the root and foundation of piety only when joined with reverence, holy prayers, and almsgiving, because God desires abstinence from evil deeds rather than mere abstinence from bread and water. Hesychius contrasts a praiseworthy fast with a blameworthy fast through biblical examples: the Ninevites were saved by fasting, while Jezebel and the Jews used fasting to commit murder. He then presents a long catalogue of biblical figures whose fasting brought deliverance, healing, or divine favor, culminating in Moses, whose fast granted him the unique vision of God. The homily closes by urging the congregation to embrace fasting with joy, to combine it with mercy and peace, and to fast from all evils, not only from foods.

outline.move: Defines true fasting as abstinence from evil deeds accompanied by reverence, prayer, and almsgiving, and distinguishes a praiseworthy fast from a blameworthy one.

Cites biblical examples of fasting: the Ninevites' salvation, the Jews' murderous plot against Paul, Jezebel's killing of Naboth, Daniel in the lions' den, the three youths in the furnace, Jonah and the sea monster, David, Elijah, Jesus, Joshua son of Nun, and the apostles' poverty and authority, with Peter and John going up to the temple to pray.

Continues the healing of the lame man by Peter in the name of Jesus Christ, then presents Christ as the one physician who heals various diseases of the soul through fasting, and praises fasting for making the barren fruitful, as with Hannah and Samuel.

Extols fasting's power to dry up lust, open barren wombs, uproot sinful thoughts, soften the hard-hearted, and culminates with Moses' forty-day fast and vision of God, then exhorts the congregation to fast from all evils with joy, mercy, and peace, ending with a doxology.

cast.name: Hesychius of Jerusalem
cast.who: The preacher, identified as a presbyter of Jerusalem.

cast.name: Ninevites
cast.who: Inhabitants of Nineveh whose fasting averted the city's destruction.

cast.name: Jews
cast.who: Those who plotted to kill the apostle Paul while fasting.

cast.name: Jezebel
cast.who: Queen who proclaimed a fast and then had Naboth killed to seize his vineyard.

cast.name: Naboth
cast.who: The poor man whose vineyard Jezebel seized after having him killed.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: Prophet thrown into the lions' den, where he cried out to the Lord and was preserved.

cast.name: Jonah
cast.who: Prophet swallowed by the sea monster, which fasted and preserved him as a deposit.

cast.name: David
cast.who: King whose fasting and repentance obtained forgiveness for his sin concerning Uriah's wife.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: Prophet who fasted forty days and received the keys of heaven to withhold and bring rain.

cast.name: Jesus
cast.who: The Savior, who fasted forty days and put the devil to shame; also named in Peter's healing formula.

cast.name: Joshua son of Nun
cast.who: Leader who fasted and commanded the sun and moon.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: Apostle who healed the lame man at the temple gate in the name of Jesus Christ.

cast.name: John
cast.who: Apostle who went up to the temple with Peter at the ninth hour to pray.

cast.name: Hannah
cast.who: The barren woman whose weeping and fasting obtained the prophet Samuel.

cast.name: Samuel
cast.who: The prophet given to the barren Hannah as a reward of fasting.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Prophet who fasted forty days and nights, entered the darkness, and saw God face to face.

key_terms.sense: Fasting, understood not merely as abstinence from food but as a God-pleasing practice joined with prayer, almsgiving, and avoidance of evil.
Almsgiving or deeds of mercy, an essential companion to true fasting.
Repentance, the change of heart that makes fasting effective.
A blameworthy fast, one that is merely external or joined with evil deeds.
A praiseworthy fast, one that is God-pleasing and joined with virtue.
Sin, especially the evil deeds and passions from which true fasting abstains.
Physician, used of Christ as the healer of souls and bodies, and of fasting as a remedy.
A healing place or clinic, used metaphorically for the places where Christ heals through fasting.
A plaster or poultice, used metaphorically for the healing remedy fasting provides for the wound of sin.
A medicine or drug, used metaphorically for the healing power of fasting against the stench of fornication.
A deposit or trust, used of Jonah entrusted to the sea monster and restored intact.
Barrenness, used literally of Hannah and metaphorically of the soul's unfruitfulness that fasting can heal.
Holiness or sanctification, without which no one will see the Lord.

scripture: The author cites the Septuagint (LXX) and follows its book names and Psalm numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and LXX Psalm numbering where applicable, with a note if the numbering differs from the Hebrew. For example, 'Jesus son of Nave' corresponds to Joshua.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is not stated in the source.
The specific liturgical occasion for the homily is not explicitly identified in the source.
The precise identity of the 'prophet' quoted in section 2 is not named in the source, though the context suggests Jonah.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐνήστευσεν Ἰησοῦς ὁ τοῦ Ναυὴ καὶ τῷ ἡλίῳ καὶ τῇ σελήνῃ ἐπέταξεν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The form 'Ἰησοῦς Χριστοῦ' appears only in Peter's healing formula (section 6), referring to Jesus Christ the Savior, not to Joshua son of Nun. The source form 'Ἰησοῦς ὁ τοῦ Ναυὴ' refers to Joshua son of Nun, a distinct figure. The cast entry for Jesus should not include 'Ἰησοῦς ὁ τοῦ Ναυὴ' and should clarify that 'Ἰησοῦς Χριστοῦ' appears in the quoted speech of Peter, not as a self-reference by Jesus.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jesus: 'also named in Peter's healing formula'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The name 'Jesus' in Peter's formula is 'Ἰησοῦς Χριστοῦ' (Jesus Christ), which is the same person as the Savior, but the brief should clarify this is a quotation by Peter, not Jesus speaking. The current phrasing is slightly misleading about the voice attribution.

_unresolved_facts.claim: John: 'Apostle who went up to the temple with Peter at the ninth hour to pray'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πέτρος γάρ, φησίν, καὶ Ἰωάννης περὶ ὥραν ἐνάτην ἀνῆλθον εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν προσεύξασθαι.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source mentions John going up to the temple with Peter, but does not explicitly identify John as 'the apostle' in this context (though this is implied). More importantly, the source does not say John spoke or healed the lame man; Peter alone speaks and acts. The brief should note that John's role is passive in this narrative.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Naboth: 'The poor man whose vineyard Jezebel seized after having him killed'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source calls Naboth 'the poor man' (τοῦ πένητος), not merely 'poor man' as an afterthought. The brief accurately captures this, but should note that the source emphasizes his poverty as part of the injustice.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Hesychius contrasts a praiseworthy fast with a blameworthy fast through biblical examples: the Ninevites were saved by fasting, while Jezebel and the Jews used fasting to commit murder
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πολλοὶ νηστεύσαντες φόνους εἰργάσαντο καὶ πολλοὶ νηστεύσαντες ἄλλους ἔσωσαν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The contrast is introduced generally ('many...many'), not as a direct juxtaposition of Ninevites vs. Jezebel/Jews specifically. The Ninevites are the first positive example, but the negative examples include both the Jews plotting against Paul and Jezebel killing Naboth. The argument should reflect that the contrast is broader and the examples are presented as a catalogue, not a strict binary.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-close move: 'culminates with Moses' forty-day fast and vision of God'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: 9 Αὕτη οὐ μόνον ἁμαρτωλοῖς χρήσιμος, ἀλλ' ἤδη καὶ δικαίοις εἰς καιρὸν ἐπιτήδειος, ὡς προεδείξαμεν. Νηστεύσας Μωυσῆς...
_unresolved_facts.fix: Moses is presented as one example among many in the catalogue, not as the culmination. The section begins by continuing the praise of fasting's powers from section 8 (drying up lust, opening barren wombs, etc.), then adds Moses as another example of fasting's benefit for the righteous. The true culmination is the final exhortation in section 10 with the doxology, not Moses per se.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Moses: 'Prophet who fasted forty days and nights, entered the darkness, and saw God face to face'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἶδεν θεὸν ὡς οὐδενὶ ἀνθρώπων ἐγγέγονεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says Moses saw God 'as has happened to no other human' (ὡς οὐδενὶ ἀνθρώπων ἐγγέγονεν), not 'face to face' as a description of what Moses saw. The 'face to face' (πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον) is in the quoted divine speech about Moses, not Hesychius's own description. The brief conflates the quotation with the narrative description.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The prophet (quoted): 'The prophet is not named in the source; the context suggests the speaker of Jonah 3:4, but 'Jonah' is not explicitly identified'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: φησὶν γὰρ ὁ προφήτης· «Ἔτι τρεῖς ἡμέραι καὶ Νινευὴ καταστραφήσεται.»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief's uncertainty note is accurate, but the voice entry should also note that the prophet's quotation includes extensive interpretive expansion by Hesychius himself (the explanation of 'ἔτι' vs. 'μετὰ' and the Trinitarian interpretation), not just the biblical quotation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The homily closes by urging the congregation to embrace fasting with joy, to combine it with mercy and peace, and to fast from all evils, not only from foods
_unresolved_facts.fix: The closing exhortation also includes warnings against hypocrisy (not being humble-faced to people while proud in soul to God), against stealing while giving to the poor, and against flattering God with words while killing brothers in deed. The brief should mention these specific anti-hypocrisy warnings, not just the positive exhortations.
